title: Kidneys
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 25.2 Gross Anatomy of Urine Transport; 25.3 Gross Anatomy of the Kidney; 25.10; 17.10

main.t: Two bean-shaped organs at the back of the abdomen that filter the blood and make urine.
main.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The kidneys’ bean shape.

simpler.t: Your kidneys clean your blood and turn the waste into urine.

deeper.t: They also help control blood pressure, make erythropoietin and activate vitamin D.

facts.t: They lie either side of the spine, behind the peritoneum, protected by muscle, fat and ribs.
The left kidney is at about T12 to L3; the right is lower, pushed down by the liver.

simpler.t: They sit against your back muscles, just under your lowest ribs.

deeper.t: The eleventh and twelfth ribs partly protect their upper portions.

items.name: Cortex
items.t: The lighter outer region, holding all the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules.

items.name: Medulla
items.t: The inner region, with renal pyramids and papillae.

items.name: Renal pelvis
items.t: The funnel formed from the calyces; it narrows into the ureter.

items.name: Hilum
items.t: Where vessels, nerves, lymphatics and the ureter enter and leave.

items.name: Capsule and fat
items.t: A fibrous capsule, a cushioning fat pad and renal fascia surround each kidney.

simpler.t: An outer cortex, an inner medulla and a funnel that collects the urine.

deeper.t: About 1.3 million nephrons in each kidney do the filtering.

facts.t: Each nephron starts with a glomerulus, a tuft of high-pressure capillaries inside Bowman’s capsule.
They receive about 25 percent of the cardiac output at rest.
Smooth muscle in the renal pelvis and ureter moves urine on by peristalsis.

simpler.t: Lots of blood flows through tiny filters, and muscle squeezes the urine down to the bladder.

items.name: Adrenal gland
items.t: Sits on top of each kidney; its aldosterone makes the kidney keep sodium.

items.name: Renal vein
items.t: Returns cleansed blood straight to the inferior vena cava.

items.name: Ureter
items.t: About 30 cm long; carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder.

items.name: Liver
items.t: Pushes the right kidney a little lower than the left.

simpler.t: Blood comes from the aorta and goes back to the vena cava; urine goes down the ureter.

facts.t: They develop in the pelvis and rise to their adult position in the abdomen.
facts.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). The development of the kidneys.

facts.t: The male kidney is usually a little larger than the female.

items.damaged: The kidneys’ filtering and their hormone roles.
items.cannotDo: Keep enough red blood cells, or absorb calcium normally.
items.why: Failing kidneys make too little erythropoietin and active vitamin D.

items.injury: Glomeruli damaged by an autoimmune illness.
items.damaged: The glomerular filter, which lets protein through.
items.cannotDo: Keep protein in the blood: it is lost in the urine, and oedema spreads.
items.why: Low plasma protein lets water move out of the blood into the tissues.

items.q: Explain why the right kidney lies lower than the left.
model: Both lie behind the peritoneum either side of the spine.
The liver sits above the right kidney.
It displaces the right kidney slightly downwards.
So the left is at about T12 to L3 and the right a little lower.

items.q: Compare the renal cortex and medulla.
model: The cortex is outer and lighter.
It holds the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules.
The medulla is inner, with pyramids and papillae.
Its papillae carry urine to the calyces.

items.q: Predict a blood change in long-term kidney failure.
model: Erythropoietin stimulates red blood cell formation.
Failing kidneys make too little of it.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). Anaemia in kidney failure.

check.stem: At about which vertebral levels is the left kidney?
check.why: The left kidney is at about T12 to L3; the right is lower.

check.stem: Which hormone do the kidneys make that stimulates red blood cell formation?

check.why: All renal corpuscles lie in the cortex.
